articles.title: How to be unemployed: Glenn Kelman on life after Redfin
articles.author: Glenn Kelman
paras: After 20 years at Redfin, and 10 months of unemployment, I’ve co-founded a new company. My business partner and I will announce our plans after we’ve built our product, but in the meantime GeekWire asked me to explain what I learned in the transition between Redfin and this new venture.
Many of us are in transition because society is in transition, with AI hollowing out big companies and making it easier to start new companies.

In the past, my own transitions had been harrowing, because I ran out of money or lost my sense of purpose. Leaving Redfin, I thought “here we go again.” I felt self-conscious being in the grocery store at 11 a.m. on a weekday. I was ashamed when I couldn’t come up with an idea for a company. But I made it to the other side.

To do that, I had to convince myself that I was an intrepid explorer, even if what I was exploring wasn’t Mount Everest, but instead what I could be. I wanted to feel brave about encounters I otherwise would’ve found embarrassing. Over the last year, I met people about becoming a high school teacher, a Whistler bagel shopkeeper, a candidate for the state legislature, the founder of a tree-planting nonprofit, the CEO of a pre-IPO company and a project leader for Sound Transit.
The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.

At the beginning of my exploration, a CEO recruiter told me the startup scene in Seattle was “dead” and that, for all of Seattle’s talent, more companies were forming in New York and even LA. I Googled “high-growth Seattle startups” and the list included one company that went bankrupt in 2023, and Redfin, which was acquired in 2025.

Another friend told me that she was on a Discord channel with a bunch of CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at businesses with legacy codebases. At least for me, the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.

It took me months to feel ready to do that. In January, a friend told me I wasn’t allowed to make any big decisions until September. Another said I had to wait until the frenzy of my last job had subsided. “You’ll know it has happened,” he said, “because food will start tasting better” (it never happened).

At a conference, a fashion entrepreneur who’d built and abandoned vast residences in Jackson Hole and Costa Rica, and got divorced twice in the past three years, gave me a bracelet that said “we are enough.”

Since I’d often been thinking I hadn’t done enough in the morning to deserve lunch, it was a relief to feel that I didn’t have to be creative or productive in order to justify my existence. But relieving that pressure also made it easier to be creative and productive.
On a call walking through Volunteer Park, I told a friend that the bracelet reminded me I could be happy and never start a company again. She said, “YOU JUST NEED A CO-FOUNDER.”

She told me to share flawed ideas with people who could make them better. I set up meetings with potential co-founders, and we shared our ideas before they were ready, because our meetings had become deadlines. Then we used AI to turn our ideas into products, so we could see what was good and bad about each idea. Starting a company started to feel like a natural progression, instead of Athena sprouting out of Zeus’s head.

When I confessed to a friend that everything we were working on still seemed so small, she said, “What about breakfast burritos?” She outlined her vision for a shop serving breakfast burritos all day, with a line out the door. Then she started talking about inventing a nursing home “that makes everyone happy.” Rather than running a McKinsey market-sizing analysis, she just thought about what she wanted to exist in the world.

That’s something almost anyone can do. In her living room, I suddenly felt that humanity would always have an instinct — this is a bizarre word, but it’s what popped into my head — to fructify. I remember walking home from her house with my wife and hearing the thick sound of insects humming in the night as proof of life’s rich pageant. This is what I mean by surrounding yourself with good vibes.

The last step in my process maybe should’ve come first, choosing where I wanted to make a difference. I thought about all the companies that I honestly would’ve been proud to start, and they were all in the same industry. I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing. I met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea, and a business partner who helped me think it through.

Through all of this, I depended on my wife more than any husband ever should. She works herself to the bone treating people with cancer, but she took my calls in the middle of her workday, when I would talk in detail about what to cook for dinner and then — one more thing! — what’s the meaning of my life?
Once, she was getting into our Chevy Bolt for her morning commute while I was rounding the corner with the dog, and I saw her brighten in the way many people did back when I was Redfin’s CEO.

I found myself full of anticipation. She reached into the car, as if to grab a small gift, and heaved something at me from across the street, saying it “needs reprogramming.” Before I realized it was a garage clicker, I thought she had said I was the one who needed reprogramming. “Maybe that’s true,” I said to myself, trudging past the browned lawn, and the dirty dishes, and into a world of possibilities.

articles.title: Tech Moves: Fred Hutch leader goes to AWS; Temporal, Augmodo and Neuralwatt name execs
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: — Amitabha “Guppy” Gupta , a Fred Hutch Cancer Center associate director who helps researchers translate their work to broader audiences, is leaving after 14 years to join Amazon . Starting Nov. 16, he will be a strategic advisor for nonprofit research and advanced AI with AWS’ Global Nonprofit Business.
Gupta said technology was often an obstacle to scientific breakthroughs at Fred Hutch.

“It’s the infrastructure, data, and tools standing between a scientist and an answer,” he wrote on LinkedIn. In his new role, “I’ll work with researchers and research institutions on using cloud, high-performance computing, and AI to remove those barriers.”

— Microsoft board member ‌ Emma Walmsley has been appointed CEO of HP , effective Jan. 4. Walmsley, who led the pharmaceutical giant GSK until December 2025, succeeds Bruce Broussard. Reuters notes that her seven years serving on the Microsoft board “are her closest brush with the tech sector” prior to taking the top job at the PC maker.

— Bas Nijholt , senior staff engineer at IonQ ‘s Seattle-area facility, has resigned after three years to join an AI startup that’s still in stealth mode. At IonQ, the theoretical quantum mechanics expert built MindRoom , an open-source collaboration and knowledge-sharing platform that he calls “a company brain.”

“With this new opportunity, I get to keep building and turbocharging MindRoom with a team of people who are just as excited about AI as I am,” Nijholt said , adding that the tool will remain freely available.
Before IonQ, Nijholt spent nearly four years at Microsoft.

— Bellevue, Wash., startup Temporal , whose software keeps AI agents running reliably, has named Sean Heneghan as vice president of sales for the Americas. The company ranks No. 1 on the GeekWire 200 , a list of the top Pacific Northwest startups. In September it raised $550 million, putting its valuation at $12.55 billion.
Temporal is fully remote, and Heneghan is based in the Chicago area. He joins the company from MongoDB.

— Doug Heimburger , a 26-year Amazon veteran, has changed roles, shifting from chief financial officer and vice president of Worldwide Operations to CFO/VP of Worldwide Stores. In the new position, Heimburger said he’ll help oversee efforts to improve delivery speed, reduce costs and increase growth of the Stores business. His first role at the company was data mining analyst.

— Seattle startup Augmodo has named Capri Brixey as head of retail sales. The company, which sells AI-powered wearable devices with cameras, raised $21 million in July to expand from in-store applications that let workers passively track inventory into automotive, warehouse and hospital settings. Augmodo ranks No. 122 on the GeekWire 200 .

Ross Finman, founder and CEO of Augmodo, called Brixey “the right leader to accelerate our expansion” given her experience selling to both retail and warehouse operations. Her past roles include leadership positions at Coca-Cola and Kroger.

— Meaghan Davison Praznik was named vice president of marketing for Neuralwatt , a Seattle-based startup that built a tool for calculating, in real time, the carbon emissions of individual AI requests. Her former employers include Clif Bar, AllTrails and Merino Energy.

Because the carbon intensity of grid power varies throughout the day and across regions, Neuralwatt’s technology can help customers run compute-intensive operations when clean energy is more abundant.

— BuyWander , an auction-based online marketplace for returned and overstocked retail items, has named Chris Holm as senior director of product. Holm spent nine years at Amazon, leaving in 2024 after managing last-mile and same-day delivery technology and working on Amazon Fresh delivery. He has since served as a consultant for carbon removal startup Lithos Carbon and as a founder-in-residence at the startup studio Foundations.
In August, BuyWander moved its headquarters across Washington from Spokane to Kent. The company announced $21 million in new funding in September.

— T-Mobile’s Kevin Lau has joined the advisory board at the University of Washington’s College of Engineering . Lau has been with the telecom giant for 22 years over two stints and serves as VP of digital experience engineering. He holds bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees in electrical engineering from the UW.

— Christian Smith , an Issaquah, Wash.-based tech leader, has been named president of revenue for Cloudflare , which provides security and speed services for websites and online applications. He will oversee worldwide go-to-market operations. Smith previously served as chief revenue officer for Splunk and Nintex.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Historic Transit Investments in Puget Sound
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: The past 5 days may have been the most consequential week for transit in Puget Sound this year. Across the region, voters and elected officials decided to invest in transit for years and decades to come.

On Tuesday, voters in Seattle approved the Seattle Transit Measure (STM) with an overwhelming 72% supporting the measure. The 0.3% sales tax increase will take effect on April 1, 2027 and fund 280,000 bus trips in Seattle each year for 10 years. The measure also funds 22,000 free ORCA cards for low-income, elderly, and families with young children, maintain support for Seattle’s streetcar lines, fund spot improvements to keep buses moving, and help expedite permits and inspections for Link expansion projects in Seattle. The additional bus trips will help grow Seattle’s Very Frequent Transit Network .

In Pierce County, 58% of voters approved a significant expansion to Pierce Transit on Tuesday. The approved proposition increases the sales and use tax within the Pierce County Public Transportation Benefit Area by 0.3%. With this additional funding, Piece Transit will add four new routes, upgrade existing routes 1, 2, and 3 to Stream lines, run most routes until 10pm (8pm on Sunday), and double weekend frequencies from 1hr to 30min on 15 routes. Pierce Transit will also add seasonal and special event service when needed and expand paratransit services. The additional funding will support free fares for seniors aged 65+. Free fares for seniors will start on April 1, 2027. The new routes and other changes will be rolled out in phases to allow time for planning, hiring additional staff, and buying new buses.

On Wednesday, the Everett City Council voted unanimously voted to approve the merger of Everett Transit and Community Transit. The Community Transit Board voted to approve the merger the following day. With these votes, Everett Transit end operations on March 31, 2027. Beginning April 1, Community Transit will operate all current Everett Transit routes and CT is required to maintain or exceed the existing level of service during the transition. Over the four years following the merger, Community Transit will increase service hours in Everett by 50%. In addition, CT will add a new Zip microtransit zone in Everett by March 2028.

To fund the additional service, Community Transit’s 1.2% sales tax will replace Everett’s existing 0.6% sales tax on April 1, 2027. Fares on existing Everett Transit routes will remain at $2 until at least April 2028. Any changes to the fares will require approval from the Community Transit Board.

Community Transit will pay Everett $54.5 million for the existing transit infrastructure and to mitigate any transition costs to the City. Separately, Everett will transfer $16 million in existing transit capital reserves to support replacing buses and other equipment.

Within the past week, voters in Seattle and Pierce County and elected officials in Snohomish County decided to invest in transit. The service improvements across the region will make traveling easier and more convenient for hundreds of thousands of people everyday. As Everett and Tacoma prepare for their respective Link extensions, the decisions made this week will ensure each Link extension connects with a robust bus network.

articles.title: Everett Transit to Merge with Community Transit, Bringing New Era of Bus Service
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The goal of a more unified and wide-ranging transit system in Snohomish County took a major leap forward this week thanks to a unanimous set of votes annexing the Everett Transit service area into countywide Community Transit. The move will bring the resources needed to boost bus service 50% by 2031, on top of the ability to add new routes into and out of Everett.

Established in 1969, Everett Transit is the only city-owned and operated transit agency left in Puget Sound, providing around 2 million trips per year. With some exceptions, the agency handles all local service within Everett, a setup that often forces transfers and longer journeys on trips beyond the city limits. By being annexed by Community Transit, which operates nearly five times as much service as Everett Transit, city residents will take advantage of a fully consolidated network, starting with planned service expansions in early 2028.

"We are ensuring a stronger transportation network, not just today, but long into the future for future generations," Everett Mayor Cassie Franklin said Thursday. "I'm excited that our residents who will be able to now choose public transit as a viable option to get wherever they want to go throughout our amazing county and beyond."

Under the interlocal agreement approved this week by both the Everett City Council and the Community Transit Board of Directors, the City of Everett will officially cease to operate a transit agency on April 1, 2027. At that time, the city's dedicated 0.6% transit sales tax will increase to 1.2% to match the rest of the Community Transit service area, providing the resources to enable buses to run more often and later into the evening.

"A merger of these two systems is a proactive approach. Annexation into community transit provides a clear and significant benefit for our residents," Everett Council President Don Schwab said Wednesday. "One of the biggest advantages: more service, more connections. Today, many residents, Everett residents, travel beyond our city limits to Lynnwood, Bothell, Mukilteo, Marysville, Seattle, and other destinations throughout the county. Under a unified system, routes can be planned as one network rather than a separate system. This means a smoother transfers, fewer gaps in the service and a more seamless experience for riders."

On top of concerns about the impact from a higher Everett sales tax, the annexation has also drawn worries from existing Everett Transit employees about their future at Community Transit. The interlocal agreement stipulates that no employee will be placed "in any worse position with respect to working conditions, pension, seniority, wages, sick leave, vacation, or other benefits," but union negotiations are still set to take place to hash out exactly how that plays out.

Future collective bargaining agreements will ultimately need to be approved by the Community Transit board, which will be reconstituted to include representation from the City of Everett. Transit riders are also pushing to add rider representation to the board, something that is now allowed thanks to a 2025 change in state law .

"We've had employee meetings with Everett Transit, and we've been keeping our employees apprised as we've moved through this process over the course of the year," Community Transit CEO Ric Ilgenfritz said. "We've heard the concerns of the Everett Transit employees, and they've been crystal clear about what the bar is for making sure this transition is successful. And I believe we're positioned to do that."

Service planning for the future united Community Transit network will now be able to proceed in earnest, building on work that includes the 2023 "More Transit Together" consolidation study. The guiding principles of that work include maximizing ridership by serving the areas of highest demand, expanding frequency and span-of-service, and reducing transfers. The four-year phase-in of expanded service will include a Zip Shuttle microtransit service area to be delivered in 2028, and the launch of the Swift Gold Line between Everett, Marysville, and Arlington in 2031.

"That process is where our planning experts and our consultant resources will look at the travelshed in and out of Everett, and shape a new network based on both technical insight and public input, and stakeholder input, and jurisdictional input," Ilgenfritz said. "So that process will play out over the course of next year, and our goal is to bring a new network plan to this board for consideration and possible action by the end of the year."

Getting the annexation across the finish line is a major win for Mayor Franklin, who has been making the case that Everett won't be able to grow sustainably without investing more in transit in the years leading up to light rail's arrival in the city in 2037 (Paine Field) and 2041 (downtown). Though the city has been significantly lagging even its peer cities when it comes to housing growth in recent years, Everett has a goal of adding 65,000 new residents by 2044, a fact that will require a leveling up of its transportation system.

"Our vote today is our legacy. I also think about the drivers in Everett. Everett's population will grow quickly by the thousands in the next 10 years. Just for reference, 300 cars in a road represents one mile of traffic. Think about that. If we don't do something today about generating opportunities for people to move around, then we are all going to be stuck in traffic," Everett Councilmember Luis Burbano said.

As part of the agreement, Everett will receive a one-time payment of $54.5 million, and transfer $16 million in reserves that are currently on hand for transit operations. That cash payment includes $17 million for Everett Station, putting Community Transit in control of Snohomish County's most important transit station. For a three-year period following annexation, the City of Everett will be able to continue to use the Everett Station facilities for City purposes.

Being in control of Everett Station puts Community Transit in the driver's seat when it comes to the future of the neighborhood, currently dominated by parking. For years, advocates have been pushing to rethink that area, the site of the closest planned light rail station to Downtown Everett.

"To meet the city's population growth targets, we need the station district to accommodate more housing and jobs, not simply be a parking lot with bus bays," said Brock Howell, President & CEO of Stations Unidos, formerly known as the Everett Station District Alliance.

After April 1, an 18-month interim operations period will allow Community Transit to access City resources to make the transition. Everett Transit fares, currently 50 cents lower than Community Transit fares, will remain in place for at least a year, with a fare study and board approval needed to raise them.

This week's votes, long in the making, came just as voters elsewhere in the region signed onto major transit expansions of their own. On Tuesday night , Seattle voters approved a big boost in city-funded King County Metro service via the Seattle Transit Measure renewal and Pierce County voters gave Pierce Transit long-sought funding to expand service by nearly 50% by the early 2030s.
"This is a historic moment," Lynnwood Councilmember David Parshall said. "People will long remember this day in Snohomish County as a victory for transit."

articles.title: Lin Proposes 'Orca Appeal' Carve-Out in Hopes of Resolving Growth Plan Challenges
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Councilmember Eddie Lin is set to introduce legislation explicitly allowing a pair of citizen appeals that have challenged the environmental review underpinning Seattle's current growth plan to be heard by the City's hearing examiner. The two appeals seek to require city planners to conduct a more rigorous analysis of the impact of future housing growth in the city, but were likely to be dismissed thanks to a new law approved by the City Council this summer.

The appeals date to last February, with one filed by Friends of Ravenna-Cowen and Mount Baker lawyer John M. Cary, and the other by Seattle Symphony musician Jennifer Godfrey, whose challenge has become known as the “Orca Appeal.”

With both challenges trying to hit the brakes on former Bruce Harrell's One Seattle Comprehensive Plan, Godfrey’s legal filings allege that impacts from increased stormwater runoff and declining tree canopy on the Puget Sound’s population of endangered Southern Resident killer whales were not sufficiently studied by the City. Local conservation groups including Birds Connect Seattle (formerly Seattle Audubon) and the Puget Sound Chapter of the American Cetacean Society have signed onto those claims .

Since the two appeals were filed last year, Lin introduced legislation that would remove the path of city-level appeals under the State Environmental Policy Act (SEPA) when it comes to both updates to the Comprehensive Plan and for area-wide rezones. Last month, the City Attorney's office announced an intent to ask for dismissal under that new law, which had passed on a razor-thin 5-4 margin following a contentious debate .

Lin told The Urbanist this week that the carve-out is intended to allow the process around the appeals to play out more quickly while the implementation of the Comprehensive Plan is already being delayed by a parallel appeal – also filed by Godfrey – at the state's Growth Management Hearings Board. With dismissal at the city level, King County Superior Court would have been the only available avenue for appeal – a path that could present the city with additional surprises down the road.

"We anticipate bringing an amendment to the bill to more clearly say that that [appeal] should go forward, with the idea that hopefully it can be expedited. If anything comes out of it, if we prevail, then we go along our way, and we finally put the appeal to rest," Lin said. "The worst thing, in my opinion, would be if we dismiss it and then somehow it comes back."

Getting the appeals resolved would mean Seattle could advance forward with fully implementing the One Seattle Plan, rezoning 30 new "neighborhood centers" clustered around existing business district for denser housing and businesses. Additionally, the stalled plan would upzone the immediate blocks along frequent King County Metro bus routes.
As it stands, those changes aren't likely to happen until next fall at the earliest .

Homeowner-aligned groups had been pushing for Lin to act to stop the dismissal, citing comments that he made ahead of the passage of his SEPA reform bill about not wanting the appeals to apply retroactively. But the bill included no such provisions.

"The Seattle City Attorney’s Office has confirmed its intention to seek dismissal of the Orca Appeal," read an email sent late last month by Seattle Residents for Thoughtful Growth, a group recently making a push against middle housing in the Seattle Times opinion section. "Yet before the City Council passed this legislation, its sponsor, Councilmember Eddie Lin, publicly assured his colleagues and Seattle residents that it was not intended to stop the Orca Appeal and that he would urge the City Attorney to let it proceed. The City's proposed action directly contradicts those public assurances and raises serious questions about whether the legislation is being used to accomplish exactly what its sponsor said it would not do."

Godfrey's challenge to the One Seattle plan at the Growth Management Hearings Board was heard this summer, but the effort mostly came up short in a ruling issued September 9. Godfrey and groups including Orca Conservancy, Orca Network, Puget Sound Harvesters Association (referred to as the Joint Petitioners) charged the City with faulty methodology when it comes to calculating whether tree canopy goals would be achieved – increasing stormwater runoff that could harm orcas. However, the hearings board sided with the City.

"Joint Petitioners have not shown that the [Final Environmental Impact Statement]’s discussion of existing canopy, past canopy loss, or projected future canopy loss were incorrect," the ruling stated. "Joint Petitioners have not shown that the FEIS’s methodology for quantifying or forecasting canopy was erroneous. Joint Petitioners’ cited evidence is simply insufficient to sustain such a claim."
And it wasn't just the claims around tree canopy goals that fell short.

"Joint Petitioners cited many Comprehensive Plan policies to argument [sic] that the implementing regulations were inconsistent with the Comprehensive Plan, but Joint Petitioners did not provide a policy-by-policy analysis," the ruling read. "The Board disagrees that it was the City’s burden to show how its implementing regulations 'comply' with its policies. Instead, it was Joint Petitioners’ burden to show how the implementing regulations are inconsistent with the policies. But Joint Petitioners did not discuss even a single line of text from the implementing regulations, anywhere in their brief, and so fail to meet their burden."

Instead, the growth hearings board ruled against the City by finding that the scope of the analysis conducted wasn't broad enough, and that the "maximum possible development" under proposed zoning changes would have been studied instead of the "maximum likely development." With a full year provided to conduct that additional analysis, Seattle's Office of Planning and Community Development (OPCD) has described the updates happening now as a "technical add-in" that will not change the plan in any way but nonetheless take significant City staff time to update.

Though providing Godfrey and the other appellants a second bite at the apple could present additional hurdles, Lin is hopeful that letting things play out will ultimately be in the City's best interest. Being able to fully implement the One Seattle Plan will ultimately mean clearing the decks for the next phase of zoning changes, which Mayor Katie Wilson's administration is calling " Taller Denser Faster " in a nod toward the Harrell plan's critics from the pro-housing side. That update has also been referred to as Phase 3 of the Comprehensive Plan.

"I fully stand behind a lot of the reasons why we passed the SEPA bill, and I think there is a lot of other legislation to come that it is going to be very, very impactful, I think, and help us not be subject to these delays for many years to come," Lin said. "It is a little bit tricky when there are pending matters, how legislation affects pending matters, and again, I think for various reasons, including the fact that we are already doing additional environmental review, I'm pretty hopeful that any impacts of this moving forward should be minimal."

Lin told The Urbanist he plans to introduce the carve-out in the coming weeks, following the council's budget process. If the current hearing schedule holds, arguments will take place starting on February 8, 2027.

"It's clearly been a very frustrating experience to have these incredibly long timelines," Lin said. "I'm looking forward to going bigger and bolder as part of the next phases, trying to lay that groundwork, probably more so with Phase 3."

articles.title: In Crisis Center plan, Capitol Hill’s ‘stairway to nowhere’ could finally become a public plaza
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: As the county has released details of a new, much higher construction budget for the Central Crisis Care Center set to open late next year on Broadway, there is also hope for Capitol Hill’s stairway to nowhere to finally get the community makeover neighborhood advocates first envisioned decades ago.
County officials tell CHS they will “assess potential uses” for the property’s fenced-off and empty northern triangle lot “in consultation with operators in the facility and the City of Seattle.”
“Community members have asked for green space, and the county is exploring that option,” a spokesperson tells CHS.

The fenced triangular lot where Broadway and Harvard meet just north of Madison on Capitol Hill has sat vacant and overgrown for more than 30 years. Today, the only visible structure left on the weed-covered property is a concrete stairway that once led into a building that no longer exists.

According to a history from writer and CHS contributor Dotty DeCoster , the site originally housed the Scottish Rite Cathedral , constructed by builder Frank Allen on a vacated city right-of-way. Opening in 1911, the two-story frame building featured classical pillars and Freemason insignia, serving as a hub for the Scottish Rite until the late 1950s when the organization relocated further north.

After the Freemasons departed, the building transitioned through several short-lived commercial reinventions. In late 1961, it was converted into the Music-Go-Round musical theater which folded within months. By the late 1970s, it operated as an antique store called Stop & Shop on Broadway, and during the mid-to-late 1980s, it served as a nightclub named Club Broadway .

Following the closure of the nightclub around 1988, the building fell vacant. It was demolished, leaving behind nothing from the historic structure except the concrete stairs leading up from the Harvard Ave sidewalk.
The long gone Scottish Rite Cathedral (Image: University of Washington: Special Collections)

The Polyclinic later acquired the triangular parcel alongside other nearby real estate developments. Over the years, community advocates and neighborhood housing leaders proposed turning the uniquely shaped lot into a public plaza, park, or pedestrian corridor connecting to First Hill, but none of these concepts materialized.
In June 2009 when the City Council passed legislation making it possible for Polyclinic to develop its property for a medical facility, community leaders envisioned a stairway plaza.
“That strange shaped lot could be landscaped with a staircase to bring pedestrians up to First Hill,” one advocate said.
Today, despite extensive redevelopment across the surrounding neighborhood, the property remains an unresolved puzzle.

Any development would be guided by the citizen-led Seattle Community Advisory Group formed to help shape planning for the Crisis Center and working to allocate a $3 million county mitigation fund to address street disorder and public safety gaps.
CHS reported here on the advisory group’s early work around public safety improvements focused heavily on surrounding street conditions.

Keeping area plaza spaces clean and safe has typically required investment beyond the initial development. The AIDS Memorial Pathway plaza above Capitol Hill Station has been managed with city and county funding backing management and events programming of the space.

Officials are now targeting late 2027 at the earliest for the conversion of the former Polyclinic medical building and opening for the Crisis Center, the second in a network of five county facilities providing 24-7 walk-in and emergency care mental health clinics funded by a 2023 voter-approved levy.

articles.title: Seattle’s Proposed Fire Department Cuts Expose Stretched Emergency Response System
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: I didn’t understand Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed budget cuts to the fire department until I found myself giving CPR to a dying man in Magnolia, the kind of peripheral neighborhood of Seattle that is most at risk from her call to cut firefighter hours.

It was 5:32 p.m. on that September afternoon when I heard someone collapse onto the dusty trail in Discovery Park, and saw a doctor giving a man CPR while a friend called 911. The question in that moment— When the fuck are the EMTs gonna get here? —is at the heart of the fight over the city budget that will be playing out in Seattle for at least the next few weeks.

Wilson’s budget proposes cuts from all city departments, but identifies the biggest cut in the fire department, in the form of a $7 million cut to overtime. It’s part of Wilson’s effort to shrink spending and abandon budget tricks of her predecessors that achieved a legally required “balanced budget” by creating future debts.
Wilson won’t raise taxes in the short term, and hasn’t laid out a plan for more progressive revenue. So the pie is not getting bigger, at least in this round of budget wrangling.

City Council President Dan Strauss disagrees about how big the pie is, and has released a counterproposal that reverses most of Wilson’s cuts, including increasing fire fighter overtime instead of cutting it. Much of his budget proposal redeploys those old tricks from the Harrell administration (onetime funding, drawing on reserves, optimistic budget forecasts) that put the city in the red in subsequent years. Strauss argues that “trying to correct for that in a single budget cycle can be dangerous,” suggesting that if the city is going to quit over spending, it shouldn’t quit cold turkey.

The budget wrangling over the next few weeks will determine how much cash goes to firefighter overtime, funding for gender-based violence programs, and countless pet projects from city councilors that fund public art, sports programs, and small transportation projects.

City agencies have already shared some information on fire department overtime, but not done a deep analysis of how response times could change by neighborhood if those proposed overtime cuts went into effect.

“They’ve given us averages and they’ve given us examples, but it is unclear which apparatus or engines would have additional response times because it is dependent on who has vacation, who has called out sick, and in some cases, who wants to work overtime,” Strauss says.

Seattleites are already playing this EMT-version of Russian roulette when they call 911, because the fire department already furloughs fire units when there aren’t enough staff. There’s no way to know on a given day if your closest first responders are on duty, or will punt your call to a firehouse further away.

But if you want a sense of how current “unit outages” might be affecting your neighborhood, there’s a way to ballpark it. Assuming the sick days and vacation days are randomly distributed across firehouses, it’s the small ones, with only a single response vehicle, that are more likely to be furloughed. That thinness of staffing would be compounded by cuts to overtime.
“There are some fire stations that would have a higher impact than others,” Strauss says.
And yes, I made you a map , where you can look up the closest fire station to your home, school, or workplace. I’ve marked single-unit firehouses in red.

The 57-year-old man dying before me and the other Good Samaritans in the dirt below the wild apple trees at Discovery Park day was clearly down on his luck, with black teeth and ill-fitting clothing. 911 operators marked it as a suspected overdose.
But for the most crucial minutes, he was extremely lucky.

Two doctors stumbled across him within seconds. And he was also lucky that Engine 41, the single unit fire engine operating out of Magnolia, was able to head straight for him, responding within four minutes.

About five minutes later, after fire fighters were already working on him, an ambulance arrived from another fire station in Ballard. They ultimately got him to the hospital alive but with life-threatening injuries, Fire Department spokesman David Cuerpo said in an email.
Firefighter overtime isn’t the only important issue, or even the one that has lives at stake.

The Council has held multiple public comment sessions, including one on Thursday. It’s also hearing from city departments over the next two weeks regarding public safety, libraries and education, housing arts and civil rights, tribal issues, land use, parks, transportation, and homelessness.
Whatever budget issue you’re passionate about, you can watch those presentations next week or visit the city council , though comment is only open by email per the current calendar.
The post Seattle’s Proposed Fire Department Cuts Expose Stretched Emergency Response System appeared first on The Stranger .

articles.title: King County Regional Homelessness Authority CEO Resigns
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: King County Regional Homelessness Authority (KCRHA) CEO Dr. Kelly Kinnison submitted her resignation today after only two years on the job. The announcement comes as the beleaguered agency is in the process of being partially dismantled.
In a press release, the KCRHA governing board said Kinnison’s departure reflects the organization’s changes in “mission, purpose, and service scope.” Her resignation will be effective November 16.

While Kinnison was not officially pushed out, her resignation is the latest in the ongoing fallout over the KCRHA’s damning forensic evaluation in April that found the agency had lost track of $13 million due to poor internal accounting practices.

In response to the audit, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and King County Executive Girmay Zahilay decided in July to take back administration of about $160 million in homelessness service provider contracts, slashing the KCRHA’s budget by more than two thirds.

That remnant was left in charge of coordinating the region’s $67 million grant application to the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). It also keeps several regional functions, such as holding the biennial Point-in-Time census of homelessness in the county.
The downscaling has already resulted in 10 layoffs, one voluntary departure and the elimination of six unfilled positions from the agency, PubliCola reported in August.
In a prepared statement, Zahilay and Wilson shared polite thank you’s to Kinnison.
But Wilson’s quote showed her damning criticisms of the agency’s past fiscal practices.
“I have a responsibility to the people of Seattle to ensure that financial challenges at KCRHA are addressed and stabilized,” Wilson said.
The two leaders didn’t share further details on what’s to come for the KCRHA, other than they “will make a recommendation soon on interim leadership.”

Kinnison’s resignation only further clouds the uncertain future of the KCRHA. The Trump administration has rewritten HUD’s granting criteria to disfavor service providers that follow the “Housing First” model, which the Seattle region pioneered and has heavily invested in.

HUD has already cut off funding to Los Angeles County’s homelessness authority, in part due to financial accounting issues . If the KCRHA receives a similar rejection, it could doom the agency and endanger 4,500 units of transitional and permanent supportive housing.
Wilson and Zahilay have so far refused to share their contingency plans in case the KCRHA does not receive its full funding request from HUD.

articles.title: Black Women Saved Our Empire
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: Let’s think about this for a moment. There is a lot of talk on social media about how Black women voters basically saved America from the very worst of itself . They came out not only in strong numbers, but consistently voted against GOP candidates at the highest rates (between 80 and 90 percent ). Now let’s zero in on the results of Texas’s gubernatorial race, which had hardcore MAGA incumbent Greg Abbott facing Gina Hinojosa, a four-term state rep of Texas’ 49th legislative district, which includes Austin. Hinojosa, a Mexican American, defeated Abbott by little over 7 points (Abbot: 45.7 percent; Hinojosa: 52.8 percent). She was the clear winner of this contest.

In 2022, however, Abbott defeated Dem superstar Beto O’Rourke by 10 points . What changed between then and now? And one must keep in mind that Hinojosa, a state rep, was pretty obscure when she tossed her name into the race compared to O’Rourke, a US rep. In the words of the Texas Tribune : “People weren’t exactly knocking down Gina Hinojosa’s door to get her to run for governor last year.” But in the months leading to the general election, she became “Abbott’s most viable Democratic challenger yet.” What happened between 2022 and 2026? A surge in Latino voters, and a considerable increase in their support of Democratic candidates. And this surge had a lot to do with Trump’s secret police, ICE.

Maria Teresa Kumar on PBS News said,“Latinos are not a monolith until you come for our families. And that’s basically what we saw last night [in Texas]. It was a repudiation of the ICE raids that have been happening. I can tell you that I can go around the country and there’s not a Latino, whether they work in Wall Street or they work in the fields, that don’t know someone that’s been caught in the dragnet.”

True, ICE and the utterly racist “ Kavanaugh stop ” provided considerable force to the electoral shift that played a leading part in Hinojosa’s victory and the spectacular transformation of Texas into a blue state ; nevertheless Hinojosa got only 59 percent of the votes cast by Latino men, who were 7 percent of all voters in this race . Latino women, who were 13 percent of all votes, did much better at the polls—70 percent voted for Hinojosa. But nine out every 10 Black women voted for the Mexican American candidate; and because this block represented 7 percent of all voters, they were central in turning Texas blue. (As for white voters, you guessed it, they stuck with the America-destroying party, MAGA—61 percent of men; 57 percent of women.)

To be honest, I do not have a good answer for this question: Why were Latino votes not equal to or higher than the Black ones? I can, however, provide the sketch of an answer to this question: Why did Black American women essentially save the American empire? And, yes, you must frame the 2026 general election in those big terms. Trump, by controlling both houses, and the Supreme Court, was burning the US down to the ground. It was not just with his erratic tariffs, which pissed off even our nation’s closest trading partner, Canada, but also Europe and Mexico and the rest of the world. Then there was the unnecessary war with Iran, the decimation of our empire’s military bases in the Middle East, the nonsense about Greenland becoming a US territory , the support of Putin, the weakening of the US dollar, and the non-stop corruption.

Even just days leading to the general election, it was reported that ICE paid an astonishing $495 million for a decaying and vacant prison site in Appleton, Minnesota that only asked for $75 million from the state last year. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison is now demanding Congress investigate this deal, which involves the transfer of “almost half a billion [tax dollars] to a Trump donor for a prison worth just $75 million.” The prison’s county assessed the market value of the property to be “$14.75 million in 2026.” The US was not in decline under Trump. It was falling out of the sky.

So, why didn’t Black women (and also Black men, whose voting rates were never far behind those of Black women) just say fuck it. This country hates us. Red MAGA caps are the new white hoods. And when Trump and his supporters attack DEI, they are really just attacking the small gains Black and brown people have made in this unrepentantly racist system. Why not let the whole bad business just burn to a crisp? But this is not what happened. Instead, Black women went to the polls and saved what remained of the American empire.

One reason for this curious fact is obviously found in the Black American tradition of resistance—the long and deep struggle against the racism and voter suppression that structures the Black experience to this day. This tradition places high value on the right to vote and the maintenance and expansion of our democracy. The other reason is plainly economic: If a US president decides to burn the whole country for whatever reason, then the first people to be thrown into the fire will be Black women. And so it is. Three months after Trump entered the White House, 300,000 Black women lost their jobs . By March, it was reported that 600,000 were now out of work . So, saving the US is very much about saving Black women and men and their families from economic catastrophe.

In terms of income , Black American women have lost the most during Trump’s second time in office. And so they have no illusions about the kind of monster they’re dealing with. MAGA, on the other hand, is so devoted to whiteness that its members are willing to maintain its ghostly power at the cost of all else: the material quality of life, the strength of the economy, the whole damn empire itself.

articles.title: Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest
articles.author:
<name>Eben Levey, Assistant Professor of History, Rochester Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/eben-levey-1510559"/>
paras: Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for a pope who spent two decades in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship.
As a historian of Catholicism in the late 20th century , I couldn’t help but notice that the pope’s plans walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America.

Leo plans to meet with the right-wing presidents of Argentina and Peru . He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the poorest neighborhoods in Uruguay’s capital. In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has drastically cut funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people.

And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero. A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero was assassinated in 1980 after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the U.S.-supported Salvadoran military . His ministry was influenced by liberation theology , a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru.
The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by Gustavo Gutiérrez , a Peruvian theologian and priest. He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “ A Theology of Liberation .”

Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty to liberate the oppressed . They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins. While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism.

Catholics inspired by liberation theology created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor. In my own research , I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives.

Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about analyzing society and the economy to better understand inequality . In nations like Peru, which possessed rich natural resources , liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers.
During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism.

A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism. Christians for Socialism , for example, argued that liberation meant rejecting capitalism . Some clergy, although only a handful, even picked up arms to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups.

In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – the current pope’s namesake – published “Rerum Novarum ,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution. Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies.

During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics , including some in Chulucanas, Peru , where Leo began his missionary work. Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression.

But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978. For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion. A staunch opponent of communism , he worried about liberation theology’s use of Marxist analysis. So did one of his top Vatican officials, Joseph Ratzinger – the future Pope Benedict XVI.

The Vatican began investigating some liberation theologians for violations of church teachings. In 1985, for example, Brazilian liberationist theologian Leonardo Boff was ordered to observe a year of silence – no publishing, no public speaking – to discipline him for his critique of the church’s hierarchy. Several priests were suspended over their work in Sandinista Nicaragua.
John Paul ordered that the Peruvian bishops begin an investigation of Gutiérrez – above all, over Marxism’s influence on his work . Gutiérrez was ultimately not punished.

One factor in his favor may have been his consistent opposition to armed revolution, even before violence raged in Peru from the 1980s into the ’90s. The Shining Path , a Maoist guerrilla group, was waging a war of terrorism against the Peruvian government, setting off bombs across Peru.

Under President Alberto Fujimori, the government escalated existing counterinsurgency operations, often using indiscriminate violence against citizens in the region where the Shining Path emerged. In 2009, Fujimori was convicted of human rights violations .

Leo has never described himself as a liberationist Catholic. However, his experiences as a priest were indelibly shaped by liberation theology , the Peruvian armed conflict and the church debates that roiled much of Latin America during his years there.

Leo, born Robert Prevost, was raised in Chicago. After ordination, his journey as a priest began in Peru, where he landed for missionary work in 1985. The young friar followed in the footsteps of other U.S. Catholic missionaries who had been serving among Peru’s poor and Indigenous, urban and rural, since the 1940s.

Sent to Chulucanas, in Peru’s coastal northwest, Prevost found himself in a region of pastoral experimentation. Since the 1960s, Augustinian missionaries had been working closely with the community to provide literacy education, discussion groups about poverty and inequality, and workshops to train artisans.

These programs were a far cry from the more radical actions of some Catholics who supported liberation theology. Nevertheless, the programs in Chulucanas aimed to empower the Peruvian poor, chipping away at exploitation and low wages on the region’s sugarcane and cotton estates. Like Gutiérrez, many Peruvian Christians believed that the Shining Path drew support because of pervasive poverty and inequality , and that churches could help transform the nation.

But the Catholic Church in Latin America was in the midst of another transformation. John Paul gradually appointed conservative bishops across the continent. Experimental pastoral programs lost support, and institutions that trained priests to put liberation theology into action, such as the Regional Seminary of the Southeast in Mexico, were shuttered or “reoriented.”

Yet even as the hierarchy shifted conservative, work on the ground among Latin America’s poorest continued apace. From coffee cooperatives in Mexico to human rights activists across the continent, many programs survived.

Leo’s 2026 itinerary includes multiple stops that speak to this history and on-the-ground pastoral work. The most symbolic, perhaps, is the Capilla San Óscar Romero, located in Chiclayo, the pope’s former diocese.

A neighborhood chapel renovated with donations from Leo’s connections in the United States, it is one of many sites throughout the Americas honoring Catholics who fell victim to right-wing, anti-communist violence. The day before Romero’s assassination, he used his weekly radio address to speak directly to El Salvador’s conscripted soldiers, telling them, “ No soldier is obliged to obey an order counter to the law of God .”

Leo XIV’s visit to the chapel is for private prayer, not a homily or a speech. Still, I would argue that the soft-spoken pope’s stop will evoke Romero’s message – especially at a time of strikes against suspected drug traffickers , which human rights groups have criticized as extrajudicial killings . During his final Mass , Romero pleaded, “I beseech you, I beg you, I command you in the name of God: Cease the repression!”

articles.title: Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms stands on the shoulders of Stacey Abrams, Charlotta Bass and countless other Black women who dreamed
articles.author:
<name>Allissa V. Richardson, Associate Professor of Journalism, USC Annenberg School for Communication and Journalism</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/allissa-v-richardson-1068279"/>
paras: There are elections that change the political map. And then there are elections that make you wonder whether the land itself remembers.
The auction blocks . The cotton fields . The lynching trees . The Black women who cleaned governors’ homes but could not dream of becoming governor themselves.
And now Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected Georgia’s first Black woman governor . The first Black woman elected governor of any American state.
Bottoms has traced her ancestry back five generations to an enslaved person on a plantation near Crawfordville, Georgia.
An ancestor held in bondage on Georgia soil. A descendant elected to govern it.
The same earth. An entirely different claim to power. How many women had to believe in a future they would never live to see?

Bottoms’s victory represents the paradox of Black political advancement amid racial violence and the often-unrecognized labor of women who build futures they may never inhabit. Ultimately, Bottoms’ victory reflects both extraordinary progress and the unfinished work of American democracy.
I keep thinking about the little children.

Between 1979 and 1981, Atlanta was terrorized by the disappearances and murders of Black children and young adults. Mothers pleaded for answers. Families lived in a city where childhood itself had become dangerous.

The murders unfolded just years after Maynard Jackson’s historic 1973 election as Atlanta’s first Black mayor. His victory announced a new era of Black political power. Yet that power could not shield the city’s most vulnerable children. Suspicions of Ku Klux Klan involvement circulated , although the Klan’s responsibility was never established.
That distinction matters. So does the fear.

Bottoms was born in 1970 . She was 9 when the murders began. She grew up in the same Atlanta where Black parents searched desperately for their missing children. She belonged to the generation whose futures were being stolen. And now she is preparing to lead the entire state.
What a terrible, beautiful, complicated thing.
Those murdered children were not symbols waiting to become useful to history. They were sons and daughters who deserved the ordinary miracle of growing older. They deserved a future.

Bottoms later occupied the mayor’s office that Jackson first opened to Black leadership. Now she is preparing to occupy the governor’s mansion. History has not erased its cruelty. But it has delivered an astonishing answer.
And this victory does not belong to Bottoms alone.
This victory belongs, in no small measure, to democracy advocate, legislator and lawyer Stacey Abrams . Perhaps those who recognize what Abrams made possible have sent her flowers.

Abrams ran for Georgia governor in 2018 and 2022. She lost both races . But through the New Georgia Project and Fair Fight , organizations focused on engaging voters and protecting voting rights, she helped build an electorate that could imagine Georgia differently. She registered voters, challenged barriers to participation , and refused to accept that the South’s political future was fixed.

And now another Black woman has won the office Abrams twice sought, in the third gubernatorial race in a row headed by a Black Democratic woman . There is something biblical about the path Abrams steadfastly cleared. I think of Moses, guiding his people toward the Promised Land but never entering it himself.

Abrams’ journey is not over. Nor should her accomplishments be measured by another woman’s victory. But I believe there is sacred work in preparing a future you may never personally enjoy. Some people plant trees. Some people sit in their shade. Stacey Abrams planted. Bottoms is standing beneath the branches.
And as a scholar of Black media history , I can reach even further back, to another woman who understood the audacity of claiming political power: Charlotta Bass .
In 1952, Bass became the first Black woman nominated for vice president of the United States, running on the Progressive Party ticket.
Before the Voting Rights Act in 1965, before the March on Washington in 1963, before Jackson was elected mayor in 1973 and before Abrams or Bottoms drew their first breaths, there was Bass.

A Black newspaper publisher who confronted segregation, police brutality and white supremacist violence in her four-decade ownership of The California Eagle , Bass understood that political power was about more than winning office. It was about who had the right to imagine themselves in one.

Bass ran when a Black woman entering the White House seemed almost unimaginable. Almost. But not to her. I imagine she would have loved this election. And I suspect she would have had pointed questions for Gov.-elect Bottoms.
What will you do for the poor? The disenfranchised? How will you protect the vote that brought you here?

History-making is not the same as justice-making, and representation matters. The true measure of Bottoms’ victory will be whether Georgians experience the more just state she promised to bring about .

For generations, Black women have been asked to save a democracy that would not save them. We have carried clipboards, protest signs and entire movements on our backs. We have been told to wait. To be patient. To be grateful.
And now a Black woman has been elected to govern Georgia.

The children have not returned. The past has not been undone. But something has shifted. Charlotta dreamed it. Stacey helped build it. Keisha has won it. And somewhere, another little Black girl is watching. She may not understand the history. She may only know that the governor-elect looks like her. For now, that is enough to begin a dream.
And history has taught us what can happen when a Black girl begins to dream.

articles.title: Young people turned out in near-record numbers for the 2026 midterms, with the economy top of their minds
articles.author:
<name>Sara Suzuki, Senior Researcher and Research Assistant Professor at CIRCLE, Tufts University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sara-suzuki-2776180"/>
paras: The economy was the top issue for voters in the November 2026 midterm elections, which saw Democrats win decisive majorities in both houses of Congress.

And for young voters, whether in college or not, the economy and jobs, as well as healthcare, were their top concerns, our research at CIRCLE , a nonpartisan, research organization focused on youth civic engagement at Tufts University, shows.

Overall, 27% of young people – meaning people ages 18 to 29 – went to the polls during the midterms, our Nov. 5 analysis shows. This marks the second-highest midterm youth voter turnout in the past 30 years, behind only the 2018 election cycle.

As a scholar at CIRCLE who studies young people and their voting behavior, I think it’s helpful to understand some of the factors that motivated so many young people to vote – and to cast their lot with the Democrats.
Among youth, being enrolled as a college student or not did not make a big difference in who they voted for during these midterms.

But there are some voting trend differences based on young people’s educational attainment, especially in the gap between young people with an education level of high school or less, and those with at least some college experience and more. Those with only a high school degree or less voted Democratic by a 24-point margin, compared with a 42-point margin among those with at least some college education.

College students who are young men also voted Democrat by a 24-point margin . Female college students, meanwhile, voted Democrat at a 45-point margin. A similar gender gap appears among young voters who aren’t in college.
Overall, this gender gap has persisted at least since 2024, as young women then were also voting more Democratic than men were.

About 66% of young people ages 18-29 voted for a Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives, compared with 31% for a Republican candidate, our data shows. This marks the highest percentage of support for Democratic candidates among all age groups.
Within this group, 70% of young women voted for a Democratic U.S. House candidate in the midterms, as opposed to 59% of young men.
Partisan trends among young voters have fluctuated over the past few decades – in 2000, for example, 49% of young people voted Democratic, while 48% voted Republican.

In 2026, Asian American and Pacific Islander, Black and Latino young people gave Democrat candidates the strongest support, at 81%, 79% and 71%, respectively. By comparison, 61% of white young people voted for Democratic House candidates, with 36% voting Republican.
Across race, education, income and geographic location, young people overwhelmingly indicated that the economy and jobs was their top issue in this election.
Healthcare and the Iran war also showed up as areas of importance for young voters. All three of these issues are connected to young people’s concerns about the cost of living.
We found that voting preferences did vary according to how young people viewed their own financial circumstances, a pattern that held among college students.
Low-income students were more likely than their affluent peers to vote for Democrats .
The issues that matter most to young people have shifted considerably over the past several years.
In 2020, we were seeing different groups of young people prioritize social issues like racism , climate change and gun control.
In 2022, we began to see young people prioritize the economy – their concern about inflation was the second-most important issue to them after abortion.

Now, after the economy , healthcare was ranked second for young voters. The third-most important issue was the war in Iran. This is striking, because in the past, we’ve polled young voters about foreign policy issues like the war between Israel and Palestinians and the war between Russia and Ukraine. Young people have never really ranked these other foreign policy issues as a top area of concern.

Youth voter turnout generally tends to be much weaker in midterm elections than in presidential elections. In 2018, there was 28% turnout for young people – a midterm turnout that was considerably higher than 2014, when only 13% of young people turned out to vote.

Campaigns seem to recognize that young voters tend to be less politically engaged. For example, our research shows that during the 2024 presidential election cycle, more than 1 in 3 young people were never contacted about the election. Among those without college experience, 48% were never contacted.
Our research still shows that college students face logistical barriers to voting.

Young people are frequent movers, which means they might need to reregister whenever they change addresses. The fact that college students may be living on campus while they’re registered to vote from their parents’ address can also create complications.

College students still have more voting information than young people who are not in college. But compared with other age groups, young people receive less voting information – making their turnout in the 2026 midterms all the more remarkable.

articles.title: What C.S. Lewis said about Narnia’s most famous character: the Jesus-like lion Aslan
articles.author:
<name>Christopher A. Snyder, PhD, Professor of History, Mississippi State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/christopher-a-snyder-phd-805968"/>
paras: As Netflix teases glimpses of Greta Gerwig’s newest project , an adaptation of C.S. Lewis’ novel “The Magician’s Nephew,” many Narnia fans are worried . In particular, there’s been online chatter about the new film’s depiction of the great lion Aslan: Will he really look like David Bowie , with the voice of Meryl Streep ?

For many readers, Aslan is not just a literary character, nor an ordinary hero: He is a representation of Jesus . Aslan sings the entire world of Narnia into existence and performs Christ-like acts throughout Lewis’ “ Chronicles of Narnia ,” which have sold over 120 million copies worldwide since the series’ publication in the 1950s.

As a scholar of medieval history and literature, I’ve taught and written about Lewis and “Lord of the Rings” author J.R.R. Tolkien , who were close friends and colleagues for more than 30 years. Lewis himself was a medievalist at Oxford , and both of their popular literary series are steeped in their knowledge of medieval languages, literature, mythology and theology.
Both authors acknowledged the ethical and religious themes of their fiction . Yet Lewis rejected the idea that “The Chronicles” were simply an allegory.

“ The Magician’s Nephew ,” published in 1955, was actually the last book in the series to be completed. Yet it serves as a prequel, narrating the creation of Narnia and the first appearance of its legitimate ruler, Aslan – the Turkish word for “lion.”

Later in the series, Aslan sacrifices himself to save a young British boy, Edmund Pevensie, from the White Witch, Jadis. Aslan is resurrected through his knowledge of “deeper magic,” and royal power passes to the four Pevensie children.

Christian readers have long seen the series as an imaginative retelling of events from the Gospels, intended for children but offering much to adult readers as well. Critics like Philip Pullman , who wrote the 1990s fantasy trilogy “His Dark Materials,” have denounced “The Chronicles” as religious “propaganda .”

Adding to the book’s religious appeal was Lewis’ own very public faith. An atheist since his youth, he returned to worshipping in the Church of England after a famous late-night conversation with Tolkien in September 1931.

The two English professors had bonded over their interest in Norse myths, which Lewis called beautiful “lies breathed through silver.” For the devoutly Catholic Tolkien, however, ancient myths pointed to truths, not lies, and ultimately to the Gospels. He and other Christian friends at Oxford helped Lewis come to accept Christianity as the “true myth.”

Almost immediately, Lewis began writing Christian apologetics , intellectual defenses of his faith, as well as fiction infused with Christian symbolism and theology. In 1947, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine – well on his way to becoming arguably the most famous Christian apologist of the 20th century.
But what did Lewis himself say about Aslan?

His letters and scholarly work indicate that “The Chronicles” were not meant to be allegorical . In other words, Aslan was not simply a stand-in for Jesus, and the series was not an extended metaphor.
Rather, Lewis called the books “supposals:” a way of asking, “What if?”

Aslan gives “an imaginary answer to the question, ‘What might Christ become like if there really were a world like Narnia and He chose to be incarnate and die and rise again in that world as He actually has done in ours?” Lewis wrote in a 1958 letter . “This is not allegory at all.”

Neither Lewis nor Tolkien approved of easy allegorical readings of their fiction. Both professors argued that imaginative literature was not simply the product of the author and their time , a sealed treasure waiting for a biographical key to unlock its meaning.

And both men knew formal allegory quite well. Lewis’ 1936 book “ The Allegory of Love ” established his reputation as a critic of medieval and Renaissance literature. His 1933 novel “ The Pilgrim’s Regress ” was an allegorical exploration of his own conversion, with characters that personified various abstract concepts and ideologies.

Tolkien wrote the allegorical short story “ Leaf by Niggle ” as a way to explore his own doubts about ever finishing “ The Lord of the Rings .” Like his earlier novel “ The Hobbit ,” “The Lord of the Rings” only came to fruition through Lewis’ constant encouragement.

Narnia came to Lewis’ mind in bits and pieces. During World War II, when he took young evacuees from bombed cities into his home, a lion had haunted his dreams. A few other mental pictures came to him – a faun carrying packages, a lamppost in the snow – and he began writing. Aslan “just insisted on behaving in His own way,” Lewis later wrote to one schoolgirl .

“The Chronicles” were not an allegory, he insisted, but symbolic. As he described in “ The Allegory of Love ,” “The symbolist leaves the given [facts] to find that which is more real.” Myth and symbols can, if used correctly, point to philosophical or theological truths more effectively than realistic fiction, making their created worlds feel more real.

For fans of “The Chronicles,” Narnia feels “real” in this sense – an escape to truth, rather than an escape from truth. Adapting these stories to film, however, always runs the risk of moving further away from what Lewis captured so brilliantly in his prose.

In 2018, the author’s estate sold Netflix the rights to adapt the book series to screen, and Gerwig was later tapped to write and direct at least two Narnia films. Douglas Gresham, one of Lewis’ stepsons, has an executive producer credit on “ Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew ,” and has generally been enthusiastic about the project.

Gerwig herself has expressed her “reverence” for Lewis’ work . “It was the book of my childhood,” she said at a press event in 2024. “It was the book series that I loved, and I lived through, and I spent so much time imagining myself inside of Narnia.”

Intense scrutiny of the project should surprise no one. As with her film “Little Women,” Gerwig is adapting a beloved novel . And this time, it is a novel written by a very public atheist-turned-Christian whose works have inspired the faith of countless others. Still, her “Magician’s Nephew” should not be judged by a trailer and a handful of interviews.

Lewis likely never expected that “The Chronicles” would turn into a live-action film, but he did believe in the power of imaginative art – whether ancient, medieval or modern – to move one toward truth. The virtues Faith, Hope, Charity and Prudence are frequently depicted in the medieval and Renaissance literature that Lewis loved and taught. Fans and filmmaker alike might benefit from remembering these virtues as well.
